title: BARREL: Boundary-Aware Reasoning for Factual and Reliable LRMs
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Existing models overclaim knowledge and answer inconsistently; reliable models recognize their knowledge boundary, abstain on unknowns, and answer known facts consistently.
layout: Left split-circle panel, right stacked Q&A examples, curved arrows linking them
description: The left panel is a square split vertically into 'Current LRM' and 'Factual LRM'. Concentric circles show the knowledge boundary. A pink outer ring marks unknown territory, where fabricated answers fall. An inner circle is filled with yellow stripes for volatile knowledge, and a green region marks reliable knowledge. Red dots are joined by dashed lines across the two halves, and blue arrows show the factual model shrinking the volatile region and expanding the reliable one. Robot cartoons sit at the bottom: a smiling one says 'I know everything!' and a thoughtful one asks 'What do I know?'. On the right, a legend explains Unknown (I don't know vs. fabricated) and Known (volatile vs. reliable). Two red-bordered questions follow, a Lakers question and a tree question. In each, the left robot gives inconsistent answers (1997/2014, Oak/Deciduous). The right robot answers 'Sorry, I don't know' or 'Deciduous' twice.
caption: How reliable factual reasoning is expected to improve model performance. Left: Current LRMs rarely admit ignorance and often respond inconsistently. Right: Reliable LRMs should acknowledge unknowns and express known facts more consistently.
abstract: Recent advances in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have shown impressive capabilities in mathematical and logical reasoning. However, current LRMs rarely admit ignorance or respond with "I don't know". Instead, they often produce incorrect answers while showing undue confidence, raising concerns about their factual reliability. In this work, we identify two pathological reasoning patterns characterized by overthinking that contribute to the overconfident and incorrect answers: last-minute guessing and second-thought spiraling. To address these issues, we propose BARREL-a novel framework that promotes concise and boundary-aware factual reasoning. Our experiments show that BARREL-training increases the reliability of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B from 39.33% to 61.48%, while still achieving accuracy comparable to models finetuned on reasoning data generated by R1. These results demonstrate that our pilot study is inspiring to build more reliable and factual System 2 LRMs.
